name: sender
title: A high-volume sender
summary: The relay's shape, for a server that sends a great deal - newsletters, notifications, receipts - and is judged by the large providers on its bounce and complaint rates. Everything the relay sets, IMAP and POP3 closed at the next restart among it, and more deliveries at once, a ceiling per destination and per sending domain, the feedback loops read so that one complaint suppresses the address, a hard bounce suppressed for good, the trace kept for six months and the reports receivers send about this server kept for a year.
steps: Warm a new sending address up: start with a few hundred messages a day to each large provider and double it every few days while the bounce and complaint rates stay low. No setting does this; the per-destination ceiling below only keeps a burst from undoing it.
Register a feedback loop with each large provider, and name the mailbox the reports arrive at in the complaint settings (mailbox): until then no complaint is ever read.

Give the web services listener a port (WebServicesHttpsPort) and a certificate, and publish each sending domain's _mta-sts record and mta-sts host: until then the MTA-STS policy this server hosts is served to nobody.

Set TlsRptFromAddress to a mailbox here, so that the TLS reports this server owes the domains that ask for them are sent, and AlertRecipient to a mailbox somebody reads, so that the alerts below reach somebody.

Raise [Database] NumberOfConnections in hMailServer.ini to about the delivery thread count, 50 here: the deliveries, the sign-ins and the rest share that pool, five connections as shipped, and a wait for one longer than DBConnectionAcquireTimeout fails.
Decide who may relay, require SSL/TLS when authenticating on the senders' IP range, and switch DKIM signing on per domain, as for the relay.

entries.name: maxdelivertythreads
entries.why: fifty deliveries run at once, so a high-volume sender's queue drains in minutes rather than hours

entries.name: MaxOutboundConnsPerDestination
entries.why: no destination is held more than twenty sessions from this server at once, which spreads a send without looking like a flood

entries.name: MaxOutboundPerDestinationPerMinute
entries.why: at most 120 messages a minute go to one destination and the rest wait, so that a burst cannot undo an address's warm-up

entries.name: MaxOutboundConnsPerTenant
entries.why: no one sending domain holds more than twenty-five sessions at once, so it cannot take every delivery and hold up the others' mail

entries.name: BounceSuppressionExpiryDays
entries.why: a hard-bounced address stays suppressed until somebody removes it, because a sender judged on its bounce rate never writes to it again

entries.name: ComplaintProcessingEnabled
entries.why: the abuse reports the providers send to the complaint mailbox are read and counted per domain and per account

entries.name: ComplaintSuppressionThreshold
entries.why: one complaint suppresses the address: the reader pressed the spam button and did not want the mail

entries.name: ComplaintRetentionDays
entries.why: six months of complaints, as shipped, which is longer than the week the complaint rate is measured over

entries.name: DomainReportRetentionDays
entries.why: the DMARC and TLS reports receivers send about this server's domains are kept a year, as shipped

entries.name: MtaStsHostingEnabled
entries.why: the web services listener serves each domain's MTA-STS policy, as shipped, once it has a port, so receivers can hold this server's mail to TLS as well

entries.name: MessageTraceRetentionDays
entries.why: six months of the trace, because a sender is asked about a campaign long after it went

entries.name: AlertsEnabled
entries.why: the conditions switched on as shipped - an address on a block list, a complaint rate over its threshold, a failed backup, a certificate near expiry - are mailed to AlertRecipient
